verses.text: And you hath he quickened, who were dead in trespasses and sins;
Wherein in time past ye walked according to the course of this world, according to the prince of the power of the air, the spirit that now worketh in the children of disobedience:
Among whom also we all had our conversation in times past in the lusts of our flesh, fulfilling the desires of the flesh and of the mind; and were by nature the children of wrath, even as others.
But God, who is rich in mercy, for his great love wherewith he loved us,
Even when we were dead in sins, hath quickened us together with Christ, (by grace ye are saved;)
And hath raised us up together, and made us sit together in heavenly places in Christ Jesus:
That in the ages to come he might shew the exceeding riches of his grace in his kindness toward us through Christ Jesus.
For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God:
Not of works, lest any man should boast.
For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God hath before ordained that we should walk in them.
Wherefore remember, that ye being in time past Gentiles in the flesh, who are called Uncircumcision by that which is called the Circumcision in the flesh made by hands;
That at that time ye were without Christ, being aliens from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers from the covenants of promise, having no hope, and without God in the world:
But now in Christ Jesus ye who sometimes were far off are made nigh by the blood of Christ.
For he is our peace, who hath made both one, and hath broken down the middle wall of partition between us;
Having abolished in his flesh the enmity, even the law of commandments contained in ordinances; for to make in himself of twain one new man, so making peace;
And that he might reconcile both unto God in one body by the cross, having slain the enmity thereby:
And came and preached peace to you which were afar off, and to them that were nigh.
For through him we both have access by one Spirit unto the Father.
Now therefore ye are no more strangers and foreigners, but fellowcitizens with the saints, and of the household of God;
And are built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner stone;
In whom all the building fitly framed together groweth unto an holy temple in the Lord:
In whom ye also are builded together for an habitation of God through the Spirit.

summary: The chapter begins in the middle of a sentence whose main verb will not arrive for three verses, and the delay is the point. "And you hath he quickened, who were dead in trespasses and sins" states the diagnosis first: not sick, not weakened, not badly instructed, but dead. Paul then describes the condition as a way of walking rather than a mere status — "ye walked according to the course of this world, according to the prince of the power of the air, the spirit that now worketh in the children of disobedience" — so that the death is simultaneously a captivity to an age, to a personal power, and to one's own appetites. Lest the Gentile readers hear this as an indictment of somebody else, Paul folds himself and his own people into it: "Among whom also we all had our conversation in times past in the lusts of our flesh, fulfilling the desires of the flesh and of the mind; and were by nature the children of wrath, even as others." The word "all" and the phrase "by nature" close every exit. Into that dead level ground drops the great adversative of the letter: "But God, who is rich in mercy, for his great love wherewith he loved us, Even when we were dead in sins, hath quickened us together with Christ." Three compound verbs follow, all of them shared with Christ and all in the past tense — quickened together, "hath raised us up together, and made us sit together in heavenly places in Christ Jesus" — so that the believer's biography is narrated as a participation in the resurrection and enthronement already described in the first chapter. The purpose is display over an unlimited horizon: "That in the ages to come he might shew the exceeding riches of his grace in his kindness toward us through Christ Jesus." Then comes the sentence that has carried more theological freight than any other in the letter: "For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast." Paul immediately supplies the balancing clause that is too often left off: "For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God hath before ordained that we should walk in them." Works are excluded as the cause and reinstated as the purpose, and the same verb of walking that described the old captivity now describes the new life. The second half of the chapter takes the vertical rescue and lays it on its side. "Wherefore remember" — Paul commands memory, and what is to be remembered is a social and religious exclusion: "ye being in time past Gentiles in the flesh, who are called Uncircumcision," and worse, "at that time ye were without Christ, being aliens from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers from the covenants of promise, having no hope, and without God in the world." Five deprivations, ending with the bleakest phrase in the letter. Against them stands one reversal: "But now in Christ Jesus ye who sometimes were far off are made nigh by the blood of Christ." Paul then presses the peace between Jew and Gentile back into the person of Christ himself — "For he is our peace, who hath made both one, and hath broken down the middle wall of partition between us; Having abolished in his flesh the enmity, even the law of commandments contained in ordinances" — and states the constructive purpose twice, "for to make in himself of twain one new man, so making peace" and "that he might reconcile both unto God in one body by the cross, having slain the enmity thereby." Reconciliation with God and reconciliation between enemies are accomplished in a single act and cannot be separated. Christ then "came and preached peace to you which were afar off, and to them that were nigh," and the result is stated in the most Trinitarian sentence of the chapter: "For through him we both have access by one Spirit unto the Father." The closing images pile up citizenship, family, and temple. They are "no more strangers and foreigners, but fellowcitizens with the saints, and of the household of God; And are built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner stone," a structure that is not static but alive — "all the building fitly framed together groweth unto an holy temple in the Lord" — and whose purpose is habitation: "In whom ye also are builded together for an habitation of God through the Spirit."
takeaways: Paul's account of the human predicament is triple and refuses to settle on a single villain. The old walk was "according to the course of this world," an ambient current of the age; "according to the prince of the power of the air," a personal and hostile intelligence; and "in the lusts of our flesh, fulfilling the desires of the flesh and of the mind," a corruption running inward through appetite and thought alike. Blaming culture alone produces victims, blaming the devil alone produces excuses, and blaming appetite alone produces moralism. Holding all three explains why the remedy has to be resurrection rather than reform: a dead man is not improved by a better environment, a rescued hostage, or stronger resolve.

The three compound verbs of verses five and six — quickened together, raised up together, made to sit together — put the believer's present position inside an event that has already happened to someone else. Chapter one described God's power as that "Which he wrought in Christ, when he raised him from the dead, and set him at his own right hand in the heavenly places"; chapter two says the same three things about the Ephesians. This is why the letter can move so freely between cosmic language and pastoral advice, and why it never treats Christian ethics as an attempt to climb toward a status not yet held. The sitting is the strangest of the three and the most consequential: a seated person is neither anxious nor still striving for position.

Verses eight through ten form one argument and are habitually quoted as two. "By grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast" is immediately grounded by "For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works." The Greek word rendered "workmanship" means something made, so the same sentence that denies human making affirms divine making, and the works excluded at the door reappear as the very floor the house is built on. The one thing the passage will not permit is boasting; it neither permits a Christianity that earns its standing nor one that has nothing to walk in once standing is given.

"Wherefore remember" is an imperative aimed at a specific amnesia. The Gentile converts are ordered to keep in mind that they were the outsiders, called "Uncircumcision" by others, "aliens from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers from the covenants of promise." Paul is not indulging in nostalgia for guilt; he is preventing the newly included from forgetting that they were included, which is the root of every subsequent contempt for those still outside and of every fantasy that one's place was always deserved. The phrase "having no hope, and without God in the world" also refuses a sentimental view of pre-Christian religion — the ancient world was crowded with gods, and Paul still calls it godless.

The peace of this chapter is not an attitude but a demolition. "He is our peace, who hath made both one, and hath broken down the middle wall of partition" — peace is identified with a person and enacted by removing a barrier, and it costs the abolishing "in his flesh" of "the law of commandments contained in ordinances." What Paul sets aside is precisely the machinery of separation, the ceremonial and ritual boundary markers that made Jew and Gentile two peoples; he does not thereby set aside the moral demand, since he will spend chapters four through six issuing commands. The goal is stated constructively rather than merely negatively: not the assimilation of one group into the other, but the creation "in himself of twain one new man," a third thing that did not exist before.

The chapter ends with three images that correct one another. Citizenship answers the political exclusion of the aliens; household answers the loneliness of the strangers; temple answers the religious exclusion of those barred from the sanctuary. The temple image is the most demanding, because it is under construction and growing — "all the building fitly framed together groweth" — and because its purpose is not the accommodation of worshippers but the housing of God: "builded together for an habitation of God through the Spirit." Individual Christians are not each a small temple in this passage; they are stones whose whole significance lies in being fitted to others, which makes disunity not a failure of manners but a structural defect in the dwelling God intends to occupy.

crossRefs.label: Romans 3:24,28 — being justified freely by his grace... a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law
crossRefs.why: Romans supplies the fuller forensic argument that Ephesians states as a settled conclusion, and it clarifies what Paul means when he excludes works. There the works in view are explicitly "the deeds of the law," and the immediate purpose of excluding them is to place Jew and Gentile on identical footing — "Is he the God of the Jews only? is he not also of the Gentiles?" — which is exactly the use Ephesians 2 makes of the same denial when it moves from grace to the broken wall. Reading them together shows that the exclusion of boasting is not merely about individual humility but about the impossibility of one people claiming advantage over another.

crossRefs.label: James 2:17,24 — faith, if it hath not works, is dead... by works a man is justified, and not by faith only
crossRefs.why: No text presses harder on the reading of Ephesians 2:8-9, and the two passages have to be held together rather than played off. James attacks a faith that is merely notional and produces nothing, insisting that such a faith is dead; Paul attacks a confidence in works that produces boasting, insisting that salvation is a gift. Ephesians itself supplies much of the reconciliation in verse ten, where the saved are "created in Christ Jesus unto good works," so that the works James demands as evidence are the works Paul says God prepared beforehand. The genuine disagreement between traditions is not about whether works follow but about how they relate to justification itself.

crossRefs.label: Colossians 2:13-14 — you, being dead in your sins... hath he quickened together with him, blotting out the handwriting of ordinances
crossRefs.why: The parallel is almost verbal: dead in sins, quickened together with him, and the cancelling of ordinances that stood against us. Colossians adds the image of the record nailed to the cross and the triumph over principalities, which supplies the missing middle term between the two halves of Ephesians 2 — the same cross that raises the dead also removes the legal apparatus of separation. Read side by side, the passages show that Paul thought of the abolition of the ceremonial boundary and the forgiveness of sins as one transaction rather than two.

crossRefs.label: Isaiah 57:19 — Peace, peace to him that is far off, and to him that is near, saith the LORD
crossRefs.why: Verse seventeen is a quotation, and knowing it changes the sense of "came and preached peace to you which were afar off, and to them that were nigh." The prophet's oracle promises peace across a distance God himself will bridge, and pairs it with the promise to dwell with the contrite. Paul takes the two distances of the oracle and identifies them with Gentile and Jew, so that a text about God's healing of his own people is stretched to cover the nations. The prophetic background also explains why he can say Christ "came and preached" peace when the risen Christ preached to Ephesus through apostles: the peace is proclaimed by the one who made it.

crossRefs.label: Galatians 3:28 — there is neither Jew nor Greek... for ye are all one in Christ Jesus
crossRefs.why: Galatians argues at length the point Ephesians assumes, that the law functioned as a custodian for a limited period and that its boundary-keeping role ends with the coming of faith. The resulting oneness is described in the same terms of a single new humanity, and the ground is baptismal incorporation — "as many of you as have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ." That helps explain how Ephesians can pass so quickly from the abolition of ordinances to "one new man," and it locates the unity not in a shared opinion or a negotiated tolerance but in a common clothing with Christ.

crossRefs.label: 1 Peter 2:5-6 — ye also, as lively stones, are built up a spiritual house... a chief corner stone, elect, precious
crossRefs.why: Peter develops the same architecture with the same cornerstone, and adds two elements that fill out the Ephesian picture: the stones are living and are simultaneously the priesthood that serves in the house they compose. He also draws on the same prophetic stone oracles that stand behind Paul's "chief corner stone." The conjunction of temple and priesthood clarifies why Ephesians insists on access — "through him we both have access by one Spirit unto the Father" — since a temple without admitted worshippers would be a monument rather than a habitation.

crossRefs.label: Ezekiel 37:5,14 — I will cause breath to enter into you, and ye shall live... and shall put my spirit in you
crossRefs.why: Ezekiel's valley supplies the governing image for the chapter's opening: a field of the unmistakably dead, incapable of contributing anything to their own revival, raised by a word and a breath. The vision also joins resurrection to reunification, since the next oracle takes two sticks and makes them "one stick" and one nation, which is precisely the movement from "quickened us together" to "of twain one new man." Ezekiel ends where Ephesians 2 ends, with God's sanctuary set in the midst of his people for ever, so the whole arc from death to indwelling temple is already sketched in the prophet.

interpretationNotes.claim: On "by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast," Catholic interpretation affirms every clause without reservation and reads it as the definitive exclusion of any human initiative in salvation: the whole movement begins with unmerited grace, faith itself is a gift, and no one can place God in his debt. The tradition ordinarily takes the works excluded here in the sense the surrounding argument requires — deeds performed apart from grace, and in this letter especially the boundary-marking observances that let one group boast over another — since the very next verse describes the saved as "created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God hath before ordained that we should walk in them." Because grace really transforms rather than merely covers, the good works that follow are genuinely the believer's own acts and are genuinely pleasing to God, so that the tradition can speak of merit while insisting that all such merit is itself God's gift crowning his own prior work. Justification is thus received freely and lived out really, and faith is understood as the beginning and root of a justification that includes love, since a faith severed from charity is not the living faith Paul has in view.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters read this as the clearest statement in Scripture of justification by faith alone, and press the exclusion further: the works denied are not merely ceremonial or pre-conversion works but any works whatever considered as ground of acceptance, since the stated reason is the elimination of boasting as such rather than of one group's boast over another. On this view faith is the empty hand that receives a righteousness accomplished entirely outside the believer and reckoned to him, and any language of merit — even merit described as God crowning his own gifts — reintroduces the very confidence the verse forbids. Verse ten is taken as decisive evidence that good works are the necessary fruit and proof of salvation rather than any part of its cause, and the phrase "before ordained that we should walk in them" is read as making even the believer's obedience a prepared gift. Both traditions confess that salvation originates wholly in grace, that faith is not a human achievement, that no one may boast, and that a life without good works contradicts the gospel it claims.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading gives full weight to "for to make in himself of twain one new man" and "reconcile both unto God in one body by the cross," hearing in it that the Church is not an association formed by reconciled individuals but the very form the reconciliation takes. Vertical peace with God and horizontal peace between former enemies are accomplished by one act and cannot be had separately, which is why visible communion — a single body with one altar and one shared life — belongs to the substance of the gospel rather than to its administration. The tradition draws from this the conviction that a division between Christian communities is not merely regrettable but is a wound in the thing Christ died to make, and that unity is therefore something to be restored and confessed rather than merely felt. The "one new man" language also rules out the reduction of the Church to either of its constituent peoples or to a federation of them.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters affirm the same union while ordinarily locating it in the Spirit's work rather than in institutional form: the "one new man" is created by the cross and applied by faith, so that all who truly believe are already one body whether or not their congregations share governance. Many argue that this reading takes the passage more seriously, since the unity Paul describes is stated as an accomplished fact — "hath made both one" — and cannot be manufactured or forfeited by human organisation. Some also warn that identifying the one body too tightly with a visible structure risks the very boasting of insiders over outsiders that the passage was written to abolish. Both traditions agree that the peace is Christ's own achievement, that hostility between Christian groups contradicts the cross, and that the reconciliation is meant to be visible enough that watching outsiders can see it.

interpretationNotes.claim: The clause "built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner stone" is read in Catholic tradition as describing a real and continuing structure. The apostles are foundational not merely as the source of a message now preserved in writing but as the beginning of a ministry handed on, so that the Church's continuity with them is personal and institutional as well as doctrinal; the cornerstone remains Christ, who determines the alignment of every later stone, but the foundation course is genuinely laid by particular men whose office did not evaporate with them. The tradition also hears "prophets" here as the prophets of the new covenant named later in the letter alongside evangelists, pastors and teachers, so that the sentence describes the Church's ministerial constitution rather than the Old Testament canon. The building "fitly framed together" is accordingly not a metaphor for private believers each related separately to Christ, but for a fitted and ordered communion.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally read the foundation as the apostolic and prophetic testimony rather than the persons as officeholders — the Church is built on what the apostles taught, now inscribed in Scripture, which is why the foundation is by definition laid once and not repeatedly. On this account the cornerstone's primacy is emphatic and exclusive, and any structure claiming to continue the foundational office risks adding to a foundation the text presents as complete. Many take "prophets" as the Old Testament prophets precisely to make the point that Scripture in both testaments is the base on which the house stands. Both traditions agree that the Church did not invent itself, that it is answerable to the apostles rather than the reverse, and that Christ alone determines whether the whole building stands true.

authoring.attributionNotes: Original synthesis grounded in the KJV text and the general Catholic/Christian interpretive tradition. No specific published source is quoted or cited; tradition labels denote a position, not a copied source.
